key_insight: Evaluation practices and preference-trained metrics favor overly vivid generations, so the paper benchmarks color fidelity and provides calibration methods to make text-to-image outputs match real-world photographic color distributions.
problem_solved: Text-to-image models and common evaluation paradigms produce or reward exaggerated saturation/contrast, causing outputs that look "too vivid to be real" even when realism is desired; there was no standard benchmark or calibration strategy to measure and correct this color bias.
method: Introduce a color-fidelity benchmark comparing generated images to real photography under realistic prompts and controlled variations.
Analyze biases in human ratings and preference-trained metrics to quantify the tendency to favor vividness over photographic realism.

Propose a calibration pipeline (metric recalibration and/or post-hoc color adjustment) to align generated color statistics with real-photo distributions and reweight evaluation signals toward true realism.
impact: Provides practitioners with a principled way to evaluate and correct color biases in generative models, improving realism, model selection, and downstream user control for applications that require photorealistic outputs.
visual_elements: Before/after image pairs showing original vivid generations vs calibrated (color-corrected) outputs
Overlaid color-histogram or chroma/saturation distribution plots comparing real photos, uncalibrated generations, and calibrated generations
Bar chart or scatter plot showing how human/preference metrics rank vivid vs calibrated images (demonstrating the bias and its reduction)
Simple flow diagram of the benchmark + calibration pipeline (data → bias analysis → metric recalibration/color correction → evaluation)
paper_title: Too Vivid to Be Real? Benchmarking and Calibrating Generative Color Fidelity
paper_authors: Zhengyao Fang, Zexi Jia, Yijia Zhong, Pengcheng Luo, Jinchao Zhang
